CAR-T cells derived from control or diet-induced obese (DIO) mice exhibited equivalent cytotoxicity in vitro; however, activated T cells and B7-H3.CAR-T cells obtained from DIO mice demonstrated transcriptomic alterations and diminished glycolytic capacity, respectively. Obesity significantly impaired CAR-T cell antitumor activity and durability of response in vivo, with a near-complete abrogation of tissue-resident memory T cell formation. These findings demonstrate that obesity constrains both the ability of B7-H3.CAR-T cells to control tumor growth and to elicit immunological memory, and that obesity requires B7-H3 to enable immune evasion and TNBC progression.

title: Next-generation PARP1-selective inhibition and combination therapy in breast cancer
abstract: PARP inhibitors have transformed treatment of BRCA1/2 -mutated breast cancer but remain limited by acquired resistance, restricted activity in homologous recombination–proficient tumors, and PARP2-related toxicity. This review examines two advances redefining the class: next-generation PARP1-selective inhibitors with improved therapeutic indices, and rational combinations with DNA-repair, epigenetic, immune, endocrine, and antibody-drug conjugate partners. Together, these strategies mark a shift from monotherapy toward mechanism-based combinations that broaden benefit across breast cancer subtypes.

title: Understanding mechanisms of PARP inhibitor resistance
abstract: PARP inhibitors exploit homologous recombination repair (HRR) deficiencies, including BRCA1/2 mutations, but intrinsic and acquired resistance limit durable benefit. We review clinically relevant resistance mechanisms, emphasizing restoration of BRCA function or HRR through reversion mutations, gene re-expression, hypomorphs and DNA repair rewiring. HRR-independent mechanisms, including drug efflux and reduced PARP trapping, are also considered. Understanding these pathways should guide biomarkers, next-generation agents and rational combinations to overcome resistance in patients.

title: Making resistance visible through multidisciplinary teams solving testing barriers in HR+/HER2– advanced breast cancer
abstract: In hormone receptor–positive/HER2-negative advanced breast cancer, acquired resistance to endocrine therapy (ET) is driven predominantly by ESR1 mutations, which are present in approximately 30–40% of patients, and alterations in the PI3K/AKT/PTEN pathway, which occur in up to 50% of cases. These mechanisms are directly targetable with oral selective estrogen receptor degraders (e.g., elacestrant) and pathway inhibitors (e.g., alpelisib, inavolisib, or capivasertib). However, patients who urgently require resistance testing are often the hardest to test, including those with bone-only metastases, those lacking access to reimbursement for circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) testing, and those whose previous testing targeted inadequate specimens. While technological advances, including ultra-sensitive droplet digital polymerase chain reaction and broad liquid biopsy panels, are transformative, their clinical utility is dictated by local hospital infrastructure, funding models, and laboratory capabilities. There is no universally applicable testing algorithm; instead, testing must be adapted to each institution’s specific context. Coordinated multidisciplinary team (MDT) action is essential. This review reframes molecular diagnostics as a team-based, problem-solving exercise. We present three scenarios illustrating how MDTs transform testing obstacles into actionable pathways: (1) a patient with bone-only progression and no ctDNA reimbursement for ESR1 detection; (2) a patient tested on archival primary tissue, where molecular pathology clarifies resistance-mutation timing and redirects to ctDNA; and (3) a patient with false-negative ctDNA due to low tumor fraction, where the MDT reflexes to alternative cytology (pleural effusion). Through strategic specimen selection, pre-analytical optimization, fit-for-purpose assay triage, and resource-aware contingency planning, MDTs increase detection of targetable resistance, shorten turnaround times, and close equity gaps in precision medicine.

title: Key considerations for window of opportunity trials and preoperative endocrine therapy in breast cancer
abstract: Window of opportunity (WOO) trials are short, pre-surgical trials which aim to evaluate novel therapeutic strategies and answer biological and mechanistic questions. Despite their relative simplicity, their conduct can be challenging. This Perspectives Article considers key factors relevant for the optimal design and interpretation of WOO trials in the context of oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer, and provides insights for clinicians using preoperative endocrine therapy in a non-trial setting.

title: Artificial intelligence for clinical data extraction from EHRs in breast cancer trials: the MIRROR study
abstract: Manual data entry and curation is the most used method of data collection for real world evidence and clinical trials but is a time-consuming task associated with significant human effort and transcription mistakes. MIRROR is a retrospective study that compared manual data capture from electronic case report forms (eCRF) to automated data extraction from electronic health records (EHRs) using artificial intelligence (AI). Clinical information was extracted from EHRs of 113 breast cancer patients participating in 11 clinical trials, with the system providing references to the original text for each variable to enable efficient verification. All patients were enrolled at the Virgen del Rocío University Hospital (Sevilla, Spain). Analyses provided high rates of accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score for most structured and unstructured clinical data domains. Future efforts should focus on improving unstructured data extraction and implementing standardized eCRF among sites to ensure consistent extraction and evaluation of clinical information.

title: Tubular carcinoma and low-grade hormone receptor-positive breast cancer as candidates for treatment de-escalation
abstract: Hormone receptor (HR)-positive/HER2-negative breast cancers encompass a broad biologic spectrum. Low-grade tumors, especially grade 1 luminal cancers and special histotypes such as tubular carcinoma, occupy the indolent end, reflecting morphology, lineage fidelity, genomic simplicity, and limited plasticity. This review frames low-grade HR-positive breast cancer as a distinct setting for de-escalation, highlighting multigene assays’ contribution and limits, late relapse, and the challenge of matching favorable morphology with favorable biology.

title: Viral evolution of T1L mammalian orthoreovirus enhances breast cancer stem-like cell killing
abstract: Breast cancer stem-like cells (BCSCs) drive metastasis and therapy resistance, yet selective therapeutics to eliminate this quiescent population are lacking. We explored the potential of mammalian orthoreovirus (MRV) as an oncolytic agent against paclitaxel-resistant (TaxR) ER+ BCSCs. Through serial passaging of the MRV strain T1L in TaxR tumorspheres, we developed novel viral clones (T1L SP B and C) with enhanced oncolytic potency. Notably, these evolved clones demonstrated superior killing of TaxR BCSCs despite reduced infectivity and viral protein synthesis compared to the parental strain. Whole-genome sequencing identified specific viral protein mutations correlating with this enhanced potency. Mechanistically, while all strains induced apoptosis, T1L SP B triggered markers of immunogenic cell death (ICD), significantly increasing the release of the damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) extracellular ATP. Our findings demonstrate that directed viral evolution can generate potent oncolytic agents capable of both eliminating resistant BCSCs and potentially stimulating anti-tumor immunity.

title: Hormone receptor status switch and metastatic central nervous system tropism during breast cancer progression to leptomeningeal disease
abstract: Compared to hormone receptor (HR)-positive breast cancers, triple-negative and HER2+ subtypes demonstrate greater prevalence of central nervous system (CNS) metastasis, including its most aggressive form, leptomeningeal disease (LMD). In LMD, cancer cells infiltrate the leptomeninges of the brain and spine, resulting in rapid progression, with dismal prognosis and lack of effective treatment. In this retrospective analysis of 141 breast cancer patients with LMD treated at Stanford Hospital (2008–2020), we sought to provide a comprehensive evaluation of each HR (estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR)) and HER2 receptor status at multiple timepoints between primary diagnosis and CNS metastasis, with a particular focus on the impact of HR discordance events on disease outcomes. Receptor status was recorded at the primary tumor diagnosis, at subsequent local recurrence, non-CNS metastases, brain metastases and LMD. Linear and Cox regression analyses were performed to evaluate the impact of HR status and HR discordance between primary breast cancer and LMD on disease progression. HR status at local recurrences and distant metastases, assessed by immunohistochemistry and clinical notes, was incorporated as a time-dependent covariate. A systematic review and meta-analysis were performed to compare receptor status distributions and dynamics in the Stanford cohort with published CNS metastasis cohorts. For both ER and PR, negative HR status at primary breast cancer diagnosis was associated with higher CNS tropism, a shorter time to LMD diagnosis, and reduced survival following LMD diagnosis. Since initial diagnosis, receptor status switched in 29% (41 out of 141) of patients, with HRs switched in 26% (37/141) and HER2 switched in 7% (10/141) of patients. HR loss was a predominant change after initial diagnosis and was strongly associated with increased CNS tropism and LMD. Our results confirm the value of reassessing receptor status at recurrence and identify loss of ER or PR expression as a potential marker of CNS-directed disease progression that warrants further study.

title: Construction of personal health knowledge graphs for clinical data harmonization in breast cancer
abstract: Integrating heterogeneous personal health data and maintaining clinical registries for breast cancer management is labor-intensive. This study presents an AI-powered virtual assistant transforming identifiable breast cancer patient data into interoperable personal health knowledge graphs for secondary use. The first-generation prototype was deployed across three hospitals to extract and ingest patient data under informed consent, mapped to ontology-compliant knowledge graphs, with SHACL-based structural validation and human-in-the-loop review. Curated data covered demographics, diagnosis, pathology, laboratory results, surgery, therapy, and follow-up, from which local SPARQL queries generated per-site standardized registries. Ingestion and curation results were completed at two sites: ingestion success of 51–94%, curation success of 59–64% and automated curation of 41–47%. Overall, SHACL-based structural data quality was 94.5–96.1% (validity: >98%; completeness: 76–81%). These results demonstrate the feasibility of semi-automated health data harmonization and knowledge graph construction, representing an initial step toward scalable, interoperable registry infrastructure in breast cancer.

title: Randomized clinical trial of self-acupressure for aromatase-inhibitor associated musculoskeletal symptoms
abstract: Half of aromatase inhibitor (AI)-treated patients with early stage breast cancer discontinue therapy early, primarily because of AI-associated musculoskeletal symptoms (AIMSS). Acupuncture reduces AIMSS, but uptake is limited. Prior studies demonstrated reduction in pain with self-acupressure. We examined the effectiveness of 12 weeks of true (TA) versus sham (SA) acupressure for treating AIMSS. Patients with ≥4/10 new or worsening worst pain since starting AI therapy and no recent acupuncture were eligible. Median age was 51.6 years and 83% were white. Symptoms were assessed weekly using the Brief Pain Inventory (BPI). Primary endpoint was change in BPI worst pain by 12 weeks, analyzed using a linear mixed model. For the TA group ( n = 25), worst pain decreased from 5.12 (SD 0.36) to 4.32 (SD 0.37). For the SA group ( n = 23), worst pain decreased from 5.71 (SD 0.38) to 4.87 (SD 0.51). Difference by group over 12 weeks was not significant ( p = 0.88). For those with both BPI assessments, 10 of 20 (50%) performing TA had ≥2 point improvement in worst pain, compared to 7 of 17 (41.2%) performing SA ( p = 0.59). Although joint pain and stiffness improved with TA, improvements were not superior to SA. Acupressure using this acupoint formula does not appear to be effective for treatment of AIMSS.

title: HER2; p53 co-mutated cancers show increased histone acetylation and are sensitive to neratinib plus trastuzumab deruxtecan
abstract: In metastatic breast cancer, HER2 -activating mutations often co-occur with TP53 mutations, a combination linked to poor response to neratinib and worse prognosis. To model this clinical challenge, we bred HER2 V777L transgenic mice with two TP53 mutant alleles: TP53 R172H (the murine homolog of human TP53 R175H) and TP53 fl/fl , which mimics p53 truncations common in human tumors. TP53 mutations accelerated tumor development and reduced survival in HER2 -mutant mice. These co-mutated tumors were resistant to neratinib but remained sensitive to exatecan, the topoisomerase I (TOP1) inhibitor payload in trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd). Mechanistically, TP53 mutant tumors exhibited upregulation of histone acetylation, hypertranscription of DNA repair factors, increased chromatin accessibility, and thereby rendering cells more susceptible to TOP1 inhibitors via G2/M arrest and apoptosis. This vulnerability is dependent on the transcriptional activity of TP53 mutations, highlighting a novel strategy to treat HER2;TP53 co-mutated breast cancers using TOP1-targeted therapies, which can potentially be broadened to other p53-mutated breast cancers, such as triple-negative breast cancer. TP53 mutations sensitize HER2-mutant cancers to TOP1 inhibitors via histone acetylation-mediated chromatin accessibility and hyper-transcription, supporting combination therapy with neratinib and T-DXd in TP53 /HER2 co-mutated breast cancers.

title: Genome-wide CRISPR screen identifies mutation-specific pathways converging on TAZ/TEAD activation in mutant p53-driven breast cancer
abstract: Most clinical mutations of TP53 are missense mutations. We previously showed that TP53 -missense mutations common in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) patients produce neomorphic phenotypes compared to TP53 -null cells, with the TAZ/TEAD pathway strongly associated with cell invasion in aggressive p53 mutants. But TP53 mutations alone are insufficient for full oncogenesis. We performed a genome-wide CRISPR screen to identify "co-drivers" of the weakly aggressive p53 mutation, Y234C. The loss of FGD6 (cytoskeletal regulator) and GCNT1 (glycosylation enzyme) increased invasiveness, and TAZ/TEAD activation, and the invasive phenotype was abolished by inhibition of the TAZ/TEAD signaling by either an shRNA-based TAZ-knockdown or a TEAD-antagonist. This TAZ/TEAD dependency was also observed for >85% of the top ~200 other invasion-promoting hits with highly diverse gene functions. Profiling of oncogenic pathways further identified shared and unique signaling, providing mechanistic insight into how individual co-driver mutations coordinately induce cell invasion. Taken together, these results demonstrate that FGD6 and GCNT1 mutations can co-drive cancer progression with the p53-Y234C mutation through the TAZ/TEAD signaling pathway. These diverse, seemingly unrelated mutations converge on and activate a core oncogenic process through distinct mechanisms, potentially explaining the highly heterogeneous mutation profiles observed among TNBC patients and offering a rationale for novel personalized targeted therapies.

title: Metaplastic breast carcinoma: a rare breast cancer with distinct biology and therapeutic challenges
abstract: Metaplastic breast carcinoma (MpBC) is a rare, histologically heterogeneous breast cancer typically treated with regimens developed for triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), despite distinct biology and insufficient response to standard therapy. MpBC is defined by differentiation of malignant epithelial cells toward non-glandular lineages, reflecting a plasticity that complicates biomarker interpretation and distinguishes it from non-metaplastic TNBC. In this review, we cover MpBC histopathology, biology, and therapeutic development, calling for dedicated clinical investigation that recognizes MpBC as a biologically distinct entity.

title: Tumor and ctDNA concordance of actionable alterations in metastatic breast cancer
abstract: As biomarker-driven therapies are available for hormone receptor-positive (HR+) metastatic breast cancer (MBC), identification of actionable alterations is critical for determining the optimal therapy. Both tissue and plasma ctDNA next-generation sequencing (NGS) assays can reveal actionable alterations, but the concordance between these tests has not been established. In this retrospective cohort study of 367 patients with paired tumor tissue and ctDNA NGS, agreement between tissue and ctDNA testing was high across all actionable genes. Concordance was highest in PIK3CA and AKT1 and lower in ESR1 (higher detection in ctDNA) and PTEN (higher detection in tissue). ctDNA NGS alone identified all actionable genes in 88% of patients, though sensitivity was reduced when ctDNA fraction was low. This study represents one of the largest studies of tissue-ctDNA concordance in MBC, and establishes plasma ctDNA NGS as an effective, non-invasive alternative to tissue NGS for the detection of actionable alterations in HR+ MBC.

title: Research priorities to move ctDNA assays into clinical decision making in early-stage breast cancer
abstract: Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA)-based Minimal Residual Disease (MRD) assays are increasingly utilised in early-stage breast cancer; but evidence for decision-making remains incomplete. The Breast International Group (BIG) and National Clinical Trials Network (NCTN) ctDNA working group identified research priorities to advance these assays toward clinical utility: clinical trial designs proving utility and affordability; validating ctDNA dynamics as surrogate endpoint; standardising assays; and evaluating patient-reported outcomes and equity. Prospective, randomised evidence remains essential before implementation.

title: Estrogen modulates NK and CD8 + T cell response via the PD-1 PD-L1 axis impairing antitumour effects of zoledronic acid
abstract: Clinical trials in breast cancer have demonstrated reduced recurrence in bone and soft tissue in postmenopausal women following either neoadjuvant or adjuvant treatment with Zoledronic acid (Zol). In contrast however, the same treatment resulted in an increased risk of extra-skeletal recurrence in premenopausal women. The reason for these stark differences has remained unclear, until now, preventing thousands of young breast cancer patients from being able to benefit from the life prolonging effects of Zol. Here we demonstrate that Zol induces an anti-tumor response by increasing infiltration of CD8 + T, dendritic and NK cells into soft tissue metastases, but only when estrogen concentrations are low. Anti-tumor response to Zol appears to be CD8 + T and NK cell-dependent in soft tissue, but only NK cell-dependent in bone. Conversely, elevated levels of estrogen are associated with reduced systemic and tumor infiltrating CD8+ and CD4 + T cells, increased PD-1 expression on T and NK cells, and PD-L1 on tumor cells. We propose that premenopausal concentrations of estradiol antagonize Zol-induced anti-tumor immunity, which relies on CD8 + T-cells and NK cells—an effect that is reversed by PD-1/PD-L1 blockade.

title: Immune regulation of dormancy and metastatic progression in breast cancer
abstract: Metastasis remains a major challenge in breast cancer, driven by disseminated tumor cells that persist in a dormant state. This review examines immune regulation of breast cancer dormancy across bone, lung, liver, and brain. CD8⁺ T cells and natural killer cells can promote dormancy, whereas immune suppression, niche remodeling, and systemic factors, such as aging and inflammation, may promote metastatic awakening. Understanding these mechanisms may inform strategies to prevent relapse.

title: Interpretable machine learning models for oncotypedDX® prediction using clinicopathologic data: a brazilian cohort study
abstract: Oncotype DX® (ODX) guides adjuvant chemotherapy decisions in early breast cancer (eBC), but its high-cost limits access in resource-constrained settings. We developed and evaluated an interpretable machine learning model using routinely available clinicopathologic variables to predict ODX recurrence score (RS) and optimize genomic testing. We analyzed 935 Brazilian patients with eBC from the GBECAM cohort (2005–2024). Ridge regression was selected for its predictive performance, interpretability, and computational efficiency. Patients were stratified into risk groups based on predicted probability of RS > 25, and recurrence-free survival was estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method. The model showed good discrimination for identifying RS > 25 (AUROC 0.818 [95% CI, 0.780–0.852]), with sensitivity of 0.556 and specificity of 0.859. The highest-risk quartile contained 60.8% of all RS > 25 cases (observed probability 42.8%), whereas the lowest-risk half had an observed probability of only 4.4%. These findings suggest that up to 75% of patients could be triaged without confirmatory ODX testing, reserving genomic assays for an intermediate-risk subgroup. The Ridge model outperformed previously published clinicopathologic models and may represent a cost-effective strategy to improve ODX testing prioritization and resource allocation.

title: BREST-AI: Three-year breast cancer risk prediction from screening mammograms
abstract: Accurate assessment of breast cancer risk is essential for risk-stratified screening strategies. We developed BREST-AI, a deep-learning model that predicts three-year breast cancer risk from negative screening mammograms. Model development used a curriculum-learning strategy and data from 65,419 women; the model was trained on 58,591 women (9020 cancer, 1633 benign, and 47,938 three-year cancer-free). In the external UK case–control validation (1899 cases and 5697 matched controls), BREST-AI achieved an AUC of 0.751 (95% CI 0.738–0.764), outperforming Mirai (0.700, 95% CI 0.687–0.714; p < 0.001). In a US external cohort (97 cases and 291 matched controls), AUCs were 0.670 (95% CI 0.609–0.731) for BREST-AI and 0.633 (95% CI 0.570–0.696) for Mirai ( p = 0.199); this analysis is underpowered to detect modest differences and should be interpreted as exploratory. In a UK cross-vendor external cohort acquired on Siemens systems (400 cases and 1200 matched controls), cross-vendor domain shift modestly reduced discrimination, but BREST-AI still exceeded Mirai (AUC 0.719 versus 0.685; p = 0.019). When projecting case–control results to the English screening prevalence (8 cancers per 1000 examinations), BREST-AI yielded an estimated positive predictive value of 8.0% and a relative risk of 10.1 at a high-risk operating point defined by 99% specificity. These prevalence-adjusted estimates suggest that BREST-AI could help to identify a small subgroup of women at high three-year breast cancer risk within the NHS Breast Screening Programme.

title: Matched ER+/ER− breast cancer models reveal disparate estrogen effects in mammary and pulmonary premetastatic environments
abstract: Estrogen targets multiple cell types that impact tumor progression. However, effects on metastatic processes and interplay of signals to cancer cells and stromal cells are poorly understood. Using an immunocompetent preclinical model of estrogen receptor alpha (ER + ) breast cancer and two matched CRISPR-Cas9 Esr1 -ablated (ER-) cell lines, we demonstrate that supplemental 17β-estradiol fosters a pro-tumor immune environment for both ER+ and ER- mammary tumors, but exerts disparate effects on early pulmonary colonization following intravenous injection: promoting ER + , but inhibiting ER- tumor lesions. Interrogation of mammary tumor environments and splenic and pulmonary immune cells revealed marked effects of 17β-estradiol on immune subpopulations and activity. RNASeq analyses illuminated the potential of ER+ tumor cells for immune evasion, revealing a new facet of estrogen action in ER+ cancer. This context-specific interplay among estrogen responsive cells in the mammary and premetastatic pulmonary environments has implications beyond breast cancers, including ER- cancers of varying origins.
